The upcoming MacBook Ultra is sure to come with a hefty price tag, packing a brand-new slim design, an OLED display with touch capabilities — and that's before you factor in price hikes driven by rising memory costs. The latest reporting suggests production costs could be pushed even higher.

Apple typically sources components from multiple suppliers to ensure a steady supply of displays and negotiate the best pricing, and it had hoped to extend that strategy to the MacBook Ultra. However, supply chain sources indicate that Apple ultimately decided to go with a single display supplier…

Apple's product screens are handled by three partners: Samsung, LG, and BOE. BOE has so far only supplied displays for the company's lower-end products, while premium display orders are split between Samsung and LG.

The MacBook Ultra will feature Apple's most sophisticated display to date. Combining tandem OLED with touch capabilities and scaling it up to the larger size required for a laptop is no small feat. The latest supply chain report indicates Apple has decided to source these displays exclusively from Samsung.

According to The Elec, LG failed to meet the production volumes Apple required.

Apple needs large-area substrates for mass production. Samsung Display is meeting this with its 8.6th-generation OLED production line, while LG Display is reportedly exploring the use of its existing 6th-generation production line. Even though manufacturing laptop OLED displays on a 6th-generation production line is technically feasible, substrate efficiency and productivity are lower than on an 8.6th-generation production line. With early production volumes being lower, Apple ultimately chose Samsung Display as its sole supplier.

It appears LG can only offer limited capacity, and the logistical complexity of working with two suppliers isn't worth it. LG is not expected to be in a position to supply displays for this flagship MacBook until 2029.

This arrangement undoubtedly gives Samsung stronger leverage in panel pricing. This situation is expected to drive up Apple's production costs and, much like the ongoing surge in memory costs, will ultimately be passed on to consumers.

Given how eye-wateringly expensive the MacBook Ultra could be, how interested are you in considering an upgrade? Share your thoughts in the comments section.
